title: The servant's ear (Luke 22:47–53)
hook: even while arrested he heals the ear Peter cut off

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden: agonia, the sweat like drops of blood, and an angel strengthened him. Who did you carry in prayer, or in thought, through their own hard night? Day four hundred eighty-two.

The prayer in the garden is over. Torches come up the hill. A crowd with swords and clubs, and at the front a familiar face: Judas, one of the twelve, leaning in to kiss his teacher. In the dark it all happens fast. Someone near Jesus asks, Lord, shall we strike with the sword? and doesn't wait for the answer. A blade swings. The servant of the high priest is holding the side of his head, and his right ear is gone. This is the moment a fight starts. Everyone can feel it. Today we watch what Jesus does with that moment, and it is the last healing Luke records before the cross.
screen: `TORCHES IN THE GARDEN.` → `A KISS, THEN A SWORD.` → `A RIGHT EAR CUT OFF.`

segments.voice: All four Gospels tell of the sword in the garden. Only John gives the names: the one with the sword is Simon Peter, and the servant is called Malchus. Only Luke, the doctor's Gospel by old tradition, tells us what happened next. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "But Jesus answering, said: Suffer ye thus far. And when he had touched his ear, he healed him." Suffer ye thus far. It's an old phrase, and nobody is fully sure of the exact sense of the Greek. Many modern readers hear it as no more of this, or enough, stop here. Others hear Jesus speaking to the crowd: let me go this far, let me reach him. Either way, the fighting ends with a hand on a stranger's wound. Look at who gets healed. Not a friend. Not a disciple. A man who came out at night to arrest him. And look at when. Jesus is about to be bound, and his own hands are the ones still free to touch. Then he turns to the chief priests and captains and says it plainly: they could have taken him any day in the temple, "but this is your hour, and the power of darkness." He names the darkness. He doesn't fight it with a sword. Read slowly, the scene shows how Jesus meets violence: he refuses it, and he repairs what his own side broke. Peter swung the blade. Jesus cleans up after Peter. On an ordinary day that's the part that stings. Most of the damage we have to mend wasn't done by our enemies. It was done by us, or by people on our side, trying to help.
screen: `PETER'S SWORD, MALCHUS'S EAR.` · `SUFFER YE THUS FAR.` · `HE HEALS THE MAN WHO CAME FOR HIM.` · `THIS IS YOUR HOUR.` · then, large: `HE TOUCHED HIS EAR, AND HEALED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: heal one thing you damaged. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing come to mind that broke because of you. A sharp word in a group chat. A borrowed thing returned worse. A friendship you let go quiet on purpose. Don't make a list; just let one come. Picture what touching it would look like. A message. An apology with no excuse attached. Fixing the thing. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to do it. If not, just hold it in front of you and decide one small next step. The bell holds the time.
Malchus. The name John gives the servant whose ear Peter cut off, and whom Jesus touched and healed while the soldiers closed in. Today's word.
Your line: no more of this. Today, when an argument starts to swing, say it to yourself, put the sword down, and fix one thing your side broke. Day four hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the arrest in the garden in the Passion read on Palm Sunday and Good Friday, and the healing of the servant's ear is preached by many as Christ's refusal of violence even in his own defense.

fork.setup: you're Jesus. the crowd has come for you, one of yours has just cut off a servant's ear, and everyone is waiting to see if this becomes a fight. what do you do?
options: tell your friends to fight while you get away.
stop it, and heal the servant's ear.
say nothing and let it play out.
fork.reveal: "Suffer ye thus far." he touches the ear and heals it, then lets himself be taken. the last healing before the cross goes to one of the men who came for him.

original.note: Greek: ear, the word Luke uses when Jesus touches it. (Luke 22:51)

trapdoor: what you thought: a disciple loses his temper and someone gets hurt.
what it means: Jesus ends the violence on his own side and heals the man who came to arrest him.
what a scholar hears: only Luke records the healing; only John names Peter and Malchus. the Greek of "suffer ye thus far" is brief and read more than one way.

notes: The carry 'no more of this' is a modern rendering of Luke 22:51 (the Douay and KJV read 'Suffer ye thus far'); the script explains both. Confirm.
'The last healing Luke records before the cross': confirm against Luke 22–23.
Luke as 'the doctor's Gospel by old tradition' rests on Colossians 4:14 and early tradition; confirm phrasing.
Two readings of 'suffer ye thus far' (to the disciples: stop; to the captors: let me reach him) are given without ranking; confirm both are fairly described.
Original: ὠτίον in Luke 22:51 (Luke 22:50 has οὖς); confirm the spelling and verse.

Audit (second sample): invented details (a scream; the ear 'on the ground') removed, since Luke says only that the right ear was cut off. Vague 'the Church has long read this scene' and 'often preached' softened.
